Verify Now Blog > 12 PCB Layout Guidelines for Better Component Placement 12 PCB Layout Guidelines for Better Component Placement by: Mila Oct 29,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout PCB Layout PCB Component Placement PCB Layout Guidelines PCB Design Guidelines PCB layout involves more than simply placing components and routing traces. Component spacing, decoupling capacitor placement, pad connections, thermal management, and manufacturing constraints all affect PCB assembly quality and long-term reliability. The following PCB layout guidelines cover 12 practical details that engineers should consider during PCB component placement and design. 1. SMT Component Spacing The spacing between surface-mount technology (SMT) components is an important consideration in PCB layout. Insufficient spacing can make solder paste printing and component placement more difficult, increase the risk of solder bridging, and complicate rework and maintenance. The following values can serve as preliminary references for PCB component spacing: Same-type components: A spacing of at least 0.3 mm may be used as a reference. Different types of components: A spacing of at least 0.13 × h + 0.3 mm may be used as a reference, where h is the maximum height difference between adjacent components. Components requiring manual placement or rework: A spacing of at least 1.5 mm may be considered, depending on the available working space and tools. These values are for reference only and are not universal manufacturing standards. Actual PCB component spacing should be determined based on component packages, pad dimensions, solder paste printing, placement equipment, and the manufacturing and assembly capabilities of the PCB supplier. 2. Spacing Between Through-Hole and SMT Components Adequate spacing should also be maintained between through-hole components and SMT components to prevent interference during component placement, soldering, and subsequent rework. A spacing of 1–3 mm can serve as a general reference, but the actual distance depends on component dimensions, lead positions, soldering methods, and maintenance requirements. For PCBs assembled using wave soldering, engineers should also consider component orientation, shadowing effects caused by adjacent components, and whether solder can reach the joints effectively. 3. IC Decoupling Capacitor Placement Decoupling capacitors should be placed as close as practical to the corresponding IC power pins. This helps shorten the current loop between the power supply and ground, reducing parasitic inductance and power supply noise. When an IC has multiple power pins, the number, capacitance, and placement of decoupling capacitors should be determined according to the datasheet, power distribution network, and actual current requirements. Where individual power pins require dedicated decoupling, the corresponding capacitors should be placed as close to those pins as possible. The grounding path is equally important. Keep the connections between the power pin, decoupling capacitor, and ground as short as practical. Unnecessarily long traces or excessive vias can reduce decoupling effectiveness, particularly at high frequencies. 4. Component Orientation and Clearance Near PCB Edges PCBs often undergo routing, V-scoring, or other depanelization processes. Components near PCB edges therefore require special attention to their orientation and clearance. First, consider the mechanical stress generated during depanelization. Ceramic capacitors, connectors, and other mechanically sensitive components should be positioned to minimize stress concentration at solder joints and component bodies. Component orientation should be determined by the depanelization method, pad geometry, and component characteristics rather than by a universal rule that all components must be parallel to the cutting direction. Second, sufficient component-free space should be maintained near PCB edges to prevent damage from cutting tools or depanelization equipment. The required clearance depends on the depanelization method, such as V-scoring, routing, or mouse bites, as well as component dimensions and the PCB manufacturer's capabilities. For components that are particularly sensitive to mechanical stress, consider using a depanelization method that reduces stress on the board and solder joints. 5. Connecting Adjacent PCB Pads When adjacent pads must be connected to the same net, the copper connections and trace widths should be planned carefully. Poorly designed copper connections may reduce the effective clearance between pads and increase the risk of solder bridging. During PCB layout, maintain adequate electrical clearance between pads and select trace widths according to current-carrying requirements. For fine-pitch components, pay particular attention to the relationship between pads, traces, and solder mask openings to avoid problems with solder paste printing and soldering quality. After completing the layout, run design rule checks (DRC) and verify that the design meets the PCB manufacturer's fabrication and assembly requirements. 6. Thermal Relief vs. Solid Copper Connections When a pad is connected to a copper plane, the connection method should be selected based on soldering requirements, current-carrying capacity, and thermal performance. Two common methods are thermal relief connections and solid copper connections. A thermal relief connection uses several narrow copper spokes to connect the pad to the surrounding copper plane. This reduces heat transfer from the pad into the larger copper area during soldering, making soldering and rework easier in many cases. A solid copper connection directly connects the pad to the copper plane. It generally provides lower electrical and thermal resistance, but the larger copper area can draw heat away from the pad, making it more difficult to reach the required soldering temperature. The appropriate method depends on current requirements, heat dissipation, soldering processes, and rework needs. For high-current or thermally demanding connections, do not reduce the number or width of copper spokes solely to make soldering easier without evaluating the electrical and thermal consequences. 7. Using Teardrops in PCB Layout When a trace connects to a pad or via through a narrow junction, a teardrop can be added where appropriate to create a smoother transition between the trace and the connection point. Teardrops offer several potential benefits: Improved connection reliability: They increase the copper area at the trace-to-pad junction, helping reduce the risk of a weakened or broken connection caused by drill misalignment, manufacturing tolerances, or mechanical stress. Enhanced mechanical robustness: The wider transition can make the connection less vulnerable to local narrowing or separation. Improved appearance: Teardrops create a smoother visual transition between traces and pads. However, teardrops are not necessary in every situation. For high-speed or impedance-sensitive traces, engineers should evaluate whether the resulting geometric changes could affect impedance continuity or signal integrity. 8. Trace Width at Component Pads During PCB layout, trace widths near component pads should be selected according to the electrical and mechanical requirements of the design. For differential signals, symmetrical analog circuits, and connections requiring balanced current distribution, trace symmetry, width matching, and length matching may be important for maintaining signal integrity and circuit performance. However, ordinary signal traces do not always need to have identical widths on both sides of a pad. Trace widths should be determined by current-carrying capacity, impedance requirements, pad dimensions, and manufacturing capabilities. Avoid unnecessary abrupt changes in trace width near pad connections. 9. Handling Unused IC Pins Unused IC pins must be handled according to the device datasheet and application requirements. They should not all be connected to ground or left floating indiscriminately. For example: NC pins: Follow the datasheet instructions. Some pins must remain unconnected and should not be grounded without authorization. Unused input pins: Connect them to the specified logic level or use the recommended pull-up, pull-down, or other biasing method to prevent undefined input states. Unused output pins: Do not connect them directly to ground or a power rail unless the datasheet explicitly permits it. Pins permitted to float: Leave them unconnected only when this is allowed or required by the device documentation. For physical pins that are present on the IC but not used in the application, ensure that the PCB footprint correctly represents the actual package. Whether the corresponding pads should be connected to ground or handled in another way depends on the pin function and the device manufacturer's recommendations. Adding a pad and connecting it to ground does not necessarily provide effective shielding. An incorrect connection may instead cause a short circuit or interfere with normal device operation. 10. Via-in-Pad Design Considerations During PCB layout, placing a conventional open via directly within a pad can cause solder to flow into the hole during assembly. This may result in insufficient solder at the joint, poor soldering quality, or other assembly defects. For ordinary SMT pads, avoid placing untreated open vias directly within the pads, particularly for fine-pitch components, unless the manufacturing process supports the design. However, vias are not universally prohibited within pads. Via-in-pad is a common design approach for packages such as BGAs, where routing density and electrical performance may require it. Depending on the application, via filling, capping, or other appropriate via treatments may be needed to prevent solder loss and ensure reliable assembly. Select the appropriate approach based on the component package, via structure, and PCB manufacturer's process capabilities. 11. PCB Edge Clearance for Traces, Pads, and Components Copper traces, pads, and components should maintain adequate clearance from PCB edges to prevent damage during fabrication, depanelization, and subsequent assembly. If copper features or pads are too close to the board edge, routing, V-scoring, or other depanelization processes may damage the copper, expose conductors, or compromise electrical reliability. For single-sided boards and substrates with relatively low mechanical strength, additional attention should be paid to structural integrity and component placement near the edges. The required PCB edge clearance should be determined according to the board material, thickness, depanelization method, and manufacturer's capabilities. Include these clearances in the PCB design rules and verify them before manufacturing. 12. Keep Electrolytic Capacitors Away from Heat Sources Electrolytic capacitors are sensitive to operating temperature. Prolonged exposure to elevated temperatures can accelerate electrolyte loss and shorten capacitor service life. During PCB layout, avoid placing electrolytic capacitors too close to power resistors, power semiconductors, transformers, or other heat-generating components whenever possible. If close placement is unavoidable, evaluate the thermal impact based on component temperature rise, airflow direction, and the actual operating environment. Also consider the capacitor's rated operating temperature, ripple current, and self-heating to ensure that it operates within acceptable limits under real-world conditions. Distance from a heat source alone is not sufficient to determine whether a capacitor is safe. Thermal design and the operating conditions of the complete product must also be considered. Conclusion PCB layout affects not only electrical performance but also manufacturability, soldering quality, and long-term reliability. In addition to routing and component placement, engineers should consider assembly processes, mechanical stress, thermal requirements, and the recommendations provided in component datasheets. After completing the PCB design, perform design rule checks and verify the layout against the PCB manufacturer's capabilities and assembly requirements. Careful attention to these PCB layout guidelines can help reduce design issues and improve PCB fabrication and assembly reliability Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > Analog vs Digital Circuits: Understanding Digital, Analog, and Mixed-Signal Chips Analog vs Digital Circuits: Understanding Digital, Analog, and Mixed-Signal Chips by: Mila Sep 30,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout analog vs digital circuits analog and digital circuits analog circuits digital circuits mixed signal PCB design We often say that the world of chips consists of only 0s and 1s. But more accurately, digital circuits use defined voltage ranges to represent discrete logic states, while the real world is clearly not like that. Human voices have different volumes, light has different levels of brightness, temperature changes continuously, and radio waves do not simply jump between 0 V and 1 V. So here is the question: If CPUs mainly process digital data, how can a smartphone hear sound, capture photos, connect to a cellular network, and charge its battery? The answer lies in three types of chips: digital chips, analog chips, and mixed-signal chips. Understanding the differences between them is also important for PCB layout , because digital, analog, and mixed-signal circuits have different requirements for signal integrity, grounding, power, and noise control. （class B analog audio amplifier） Analog vs Digital Circuits: What Is the Difference? The key difference between analog vs digital circuits is how they represent and process signals. Digital signals focus on discrete states. In a typical digital circuit, voltage is divided into high and low ranges, which are interpreted as 1 and 0. As long as the signal remains within the specified range, small amounts of noise usually do not change the logic result. Analog signals, on the other hand, preserve continuous changes. The small voltage generated by a microphone, the radio-frequency signal received by an antenna, changes in temperature detected by a sensor, and the voltage and current during battery charging and discharging can all vary continuously over time and amplitude. A simple way to understand analog and digital circuits is: A digital signal is like written text. It mainly cares about which character is being represented. An analog signal is like speech. It contains not only information, but also volume, tone, speed, and many subtle changes. In other words, digital circuits are good at processing discrete information, while analog circuits directly interact with continuously changing signals from the real world. （Analog vs Digital Signals） Digital Chips: Computing, Control, and Memory Digital chips are best suited to problems that can be clearly defined and represented as discrete data. Common digital chips include: CPUs, GPUs, and NPUs; MCUs and various controllers; DRAM, SRAM, and NAND Flash; FPGAs; Digital interface and network processing chips. Digital circuits are built from large numbers of logic gates, flip-flops, registers, and memory cells. Driven by a clock, data flows and is processed according to defined rules. Their biggest advantage is their high level of abstraction. Engineers can move from transistors to logic gates, then to adders, processors, instructions, and software. This allows complex systems to be designed, verified, and optimized at different levels of abstraction. Digital chips are particularly suitable for: Executing programs; Storing data; Implementing complex control functions; Performing large-scale logic and mathematical operations; Precisely coordinating different functions within a system. However, digital circuits themselves cannot directly process continuously changing analog signals. A CPU cannot simply take the tiny analog voltage generated by a microphone and process it as digital data. Nor can it directly turn a string of binary data into the continuous analog signal needed to drive a speaker. This is where analog circuits and mixed-signal circuits come in. Analog Chips: Connecting Electronics to the Real World Analog chips process continuously changing voltages and currents. They do not necessarily focus on extremely large amounts of digital logic, but they often determine whether a device can hear clearly, measure accurately, transmit effectively, and charge efficiently. Typical analog and analog-intensive chips include: Operational amplifiers and comparators; Voltage references and analog front ends; Power management chips such as LDOs and DC-DC converters; Audio amplifiers; Analog circuits used in RF front ends. The problems that analog circuits need to solve are very much connected to the real world: How do you amplify a weak signal? How do you filter out unwanted noise? How do you keep an output voltage stable? How do you maintain performance when temperature and supply voltage change? Analog design is challenging because many real-world details cannot simply be abstracted away. Transistor characteristics, temperature, noise, power-supply fluctuations, parasitic resistance, and parasitic capacitance can all affect the final result. Digital circuits mainly need to determine whether a signal should be recognized as 1 or 0, so many small variations can be tolerated. Analog circuits, however, often need to pay close attention to the actual signal amplitude, noise, distortion, and offset. For example, for an analog amplifier, whether the output is 0.999 V or 1.001 V may affect the final measurement or control result. Mixed-Signal Chips: Bridging the Analog and Digital Worlds Real-world electronic devices need both analog and digital processing. That is why mixed-signal chips exist. They integrate analog and digital circuits into the same chip or system so that the two types of circuits can work together. The most typical bridge is: ADC (Analog-to-Digital Converter): Converts analog signals into digital data; DAC (Digital-to-Analog Converter): Converts digital data back into analog signals. The process can be simplified as: Real world → Analog signal → ADC → Digital data → Digital processing → DAC → Analog signal → Real world For example, during audio recording and playback, a microphone first converts sound into an analog electrical signal. The analog front end processes the signal, and an ADC converts it into digital data. After the digital processor stores and processes the data, a DAC converts it back into an analog signal, which is then amplified and reproduced by a speaker. A mixed-signal chip is not simply a combination of an ADC and a DAC. It may also contain: ADCs and DACs; PLLs and clock circuits; High-speed SerDes interfaces; Analog front ends; Digital calibration and control logic. These circuits need to work together within the same system, which is one reason mixed-signal design can be challenging. How Do Digital, Analog, and Mixed-Signal Chips Work Together in a Smartphone? A smartphone is a typical example of a system that combines all three types of chips. It needs to process digital data while constantly interacting with the analog signals of the real world. When You Take a Photo The image sensor converts light into electrical signals; The analog front end amplifies and processes the weak signals; The ADC converts the analog signals into digital data; The ISP performs noise reduction, white balance, and color processing; The CPU, GPU, NPU, and other digital processing units continue with computation, compression, display, and AI recognition. The overall process is essentially: Light → Analog electrical signal → Digital image data → Digital processing When You Connect to a Cellular Network The antenna receives radio-frequency signals; The RF front end amplifies, filters, and converts the signals; An ADC and related circuits convert the analog signal into digital samples; The baseband processor performs demodulation, error correction, and protocol processing. The signal path can be simplified as: Radio waves → Analog RF signal → Digital data → Baseband processing When You Charge Your Smartphone Power management and charging circuits convert and regulate the input voltage and current; The system monitors battery voltage, temperature, and charging status; Power devices handle the main energy conversion; Digital control logic adjusts the charging strategy according to system conditions. So, a smartphone is not purely a “digital device.” Digital, Analog, and Mixed-Signal Chips Compared These three types do not simply replace one another. In real electronic systems, they usually need to work together. Why Are Analog Chips Difficult to Replace? Many people see advanced digital chips with tens of billions of transistors and assume that analog chips must be relatively simple. In reality, the difficulty of analog design is not simply about transistor count. It lies in the trade-offs among device characteristics, process technology, noise, temperature, matching, and parasitic effects. Digital design can make extensive use of standard cells and automated tools. Analog circuits, however, often require repeated optimization based on process technology, device characteristics, and the application environment. The same circuit can behave differently when implemented on a different process. Even a seemingly insignificant trace in the layout can introduce additional parasitic effects, noise coupling, or matching problems. As a result, analog chip design often relies heavily on accumulated process and design experience, along with extensive verification and reliability testing. Why Do These Differences Matter in PCB Design? The differences between analog and digital circuits inside a chip also extend to PCB design. Digital circuits typically require careful consideration of signal integrity, crosstalk, clocks, and return paths, while analog circuits are more sensitive to noise, grounding, power stability, and sensitive signal integrity. For mixed signal PCB design, these issues often exist at the same time. For example, an ADC or DAC may connect to analog signals on one side and digital processing circuitry on the other. If the layout, power distribution, grounding, or return paths are not properly designed, noise generated by digital circuits can couple into sensitive analog signals. Therefore, mixed-signal PCB design often requires careful consideration of: Analog and digital circuit placement; Power and ground design; Return paths for high-speed digital signals; Noise control around ADCs and DACs; Decoupling capacitors and power integrity; Isolation between sensitive analog signals and high-speed digital signals. This is why understanding the differences between analog and digital circuits is important not only for chip designers, but also for PCB designers. Conclusion Digital chips have not replaced analog chips, and analog chips are not a “lower-end” version of digital chips. They serve different purposes: Digital chips handle computing, control, and memory. Analog chips handle sensing, amplification, and driving. Mixed-signal chips connect and translate between the two. Without digital chips, electronic devices would struggle to perform complex computations. Without analog chips, even the most powerful processor could not directly hear, see, sense, or interact with the real world. And in today's electronic devices, it is rarely one type of chip working alone. Instead, digital, analog, and mixed-signal circuits work together as one system. The smartphones, computers, vehicles, and smart devices we use every day are ultimately the result of these three worlds working together. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. A CPU cannot simply take the tiny analog voltage generated by a microphone and process it as digital data. Nor can it directly turn a string of binary data into the continuous analog signal needed to drive a speaker. This is where analog circuits and mixed-signal circuits come in. Analog Chips: Connecting Electronics to the Real World Analog chips process continuously changing voltages and currents. They do not necessarily focus on extremely large amounts of digital logic, but they often determine whether a device can hear clearly, measure accurately, transmit effectively, and charge efficiently. Typical analog and analog-intensive chips include: Operational amplifiers and comparators; Voltage references and analog front ends; Power management chips such as LDOs and DC-DC converters; Audio amplifiers; Analog circuits used in RF front ends. The problems that analog circuits need to solve are very much connected to the real world: How do you amplify a weak signal? How do you filter out unwanted noise? How do you keep an output voltage stable? How do you maintain performance when temperature and supply voltage change? Analog design is challenging because many real-world details cannot simply be abstracted away. Transistor characteristics, temperature, noise, power-supply fluctuations, parasitic resistance, and parasitic capacitance can all affect the final result. Digital circuits mainly need to determine whether a signal should be recognized as 1 or 0, so many small variations can be tolerated. Analog circuits, however, often need to pay close attention to the actual signal amplitude, noise, distortion, and offset. For example, for an analog amplifier, whether the output is 0.999 V or 1.001 V may affect the final measurement or control result. Mixed-Signal Chips: Bridging the Analog and Digital Worlds Real-world electronic devices need both analog and digital processing. That is why mixed-signal chips exist. They integrate analog and digital circuits into the same chip or system so that the two types of circuits can work together. The most typical bridge is: ADC (Analog-to-Digital Converter): Converts analog signals into digital data; DAC (Digital-to-Analog Converter): Converts digital data back into analog signals. The process can be simplified as: Real world → Analog signal → ADC → Digital data → Digital processing → DAC → Analog signal → Real world For example, during audio recording and playback, a microphone first converts sound into an analog electrical signal. The analog front end processes the signal, and an ADC converts it into digital data. After the digital processor stores and processes the data, a DAC converts it back into an analog signal, which is then amplified and reproduced by a speaker. A mixed-signal chip is not simply a combination of an ADC and a DAC. It may also contain: ADCs and DACs; PLLs and clock circuits; High-speed SerDes interfaces; Analog front ends; Digital calibration and control logic. These circuits need to work together within the same system, which is one reason mixed-signal design can be challenging. How Do Digital, Analog, and Mixed-Signal Chips Work Together in a Smartphone? A smartphone is a typical example of a system that combines all three types of chips. It needs to process digital data while constantly interacting with the analog signals of the real world. When You Take a Photo The image sensor converts light into electrical signals; The analog front end amplifies and processes the weak signals; The ADC converts the analog signals into digital data; The ISP performs noise reduction, white balance, and color processing; The CPU, GPU, NPU, and other digital processing units continue with computation, compression, display, and AI recognition. The overall process is essentially: Light → Analog electrical signal → Digital image data → Digital processing When You Connect to a Cellular Network The antenna receives radio-frequency signals; The RF front end amplifies, filters, and converts the signals; An ADC and related circuits convert the analog signal into digital samples; The baseband processor performs demodulation, error correction, and protocol processing. The signal path can be simplified as: Radio waves → Analog RF signal → Digital data → Baseband processing When You Charge Your Smartphone Power management and charging circuits convert and regulate the input voltage and current; The system monitors battery voltage, temperature, and charging status; Power devices handle the main energy conversion; Digital control logic adjusts the charging strategy according to system conditions. So, a smartphone is not purely a “digital device.” Digital, Analog, and Mixed-Signal Chips Compared These three types do not simply replace one another. In real electronic systems, they usually need to work together. Why Are Analog Chips Difficult to Replace? Many people see advanced digital chips with tens of billions of transistors and assume that analog chips must be relatively simple. In reality, the difficulty of analog design is not simply about transistor count. It lies in the trade-offs among device characteristics, process technology, noise, temperature, matching, and parasitic effects. Digital design can make extensive use of standard cells and automated tools. Analog circuits, however, often require repeated optimization based on process technology, device characteristics, and the application environment. The same circuit can behave differently when implemented on a different process. Even a seemingly insignificant trace in the layout can introduce additional parasitic effects, noise coupling, or matching problems. As a result, analog chip design often relies heavily on accumulated process and design experience, along with extensive verification and reliability testing. Why Do These Differences Matter in PCB Design? The differences between analog and digital circuits inside a chip also extend to PCB design. Digital circuits typically require careful consideration of signal integrity, crosstalk, clocks, and return paths, while analog circuits are more sensitive to noise, grounding, power stability, and sensitive signal integrity. For mixed signal PCB design, these issues often exist at the same time. For example, an ADC or DAC may connect to analog signals on one side and digital processing circuitry on the other. If the layout, power distribution, grounding, or return paths are not properly designed, noise generated by digital circuits can couple into sensitive analog signals. Therefore, mixed-signal PCB design often requires careful consideration of: Analog and digital circuit placement; Power and ground design; Return paths for high-speed digital signals; Noise control around ADCs and DACs; Decoupling capacitors and power integrity; Isolation between sensitive analog signals and high-speed digital signals. This is why understanding the differences between analog and digital circuits is important not only for chip designers, but also for PCB designers. Conclusion Digital chips have not replaced analog chips, and analog chips are not a “lower-end” version of digital chips. They serve different purposes: Digital chips handle computing, control, and memory. Analog chips handle sensing, amplification, and driving. Mixed-signal chips connect and translate between the two. Without digital chips, electronic devices would struggle to perform complex computations. Without analog chips, even the most powerful processor could not directly hear, see, sense, or interact with the real world. And in today's electronic devices, it is rarely one type of chip working alone. Instead, digital, analog, and mixed-signal circuits work together as one system. The smartphones, computers, vehicles, and smart devices we use every day are ultimately the result of these three worlds working together. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Are More PCB Decoupling Capacitors Always Better? by: Mila Oct 12,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout decoupling capacitor PCB decoupling capacitor decoupling capacitor placement PCB power integrity If you have ever designed a PCB schematic , you have probably placed a familiar trio of capacitors near a chip’s power pins: 0.1 µF, 1 µF, and 10 µF.It seems like a safe bet. Different capacitance values, neatly arranged, ready to keep the power supply stable and suppress noise. But is this tried-and-tested combination always the best choice? When it comes to decoupling capacitors, does adding more always mean better performance? Not necessarily. Effective decoupling depends on more than capacitance alone. Component characteristics, parasitic effects, and PCB layout all play a role. Understanding ESR, ESL, and Self-Resonant Frequenc Circuit theory tells us that the impedance of an ideal capacitor decreases as frequency increases. Real capacitors, however, are not quite so simple. They have two important parasitic parameters: equivalent series resistance (ESR) and equivalent series inductance (ESL). ESL deserves particular attention. As frequency increases, the capacitive impedance decreases until the capacitor reaches its self-resonant frequency (SRF). Around this frequency, the capacitor typically exhibits its minimum impedance. Beyond SRF, parasitic inductance begins to dominate, and impedance increases with frequency. In other words, a capacitor does not become more effective at filtering noise simply because the frequency keeps rising. Above its SRF, its ability to suppress higher-frequency noise may be limited. That is why selecting a PCB decoupling capacitor requires more than checking its nominal capacitance. You also need to understand how its impedance changes with frequency. How Different Capacitance Values Work Together Capacitors with different capacitance values have different impedance characteristics. When selected appropriately, they can help maintain low impedance across a wider frequency range in the power distribution network (PDN). 10 µF capacitors are commonly used to provide local charge storage and help reduce impedance over certain low- to mid-frequency ranges. Their actual performance depends on the capacitor type, package, ESR, ESL, and operating voltage. For lower-frequency ripple, the voltage regulator, bulk capacitors, and the overall power network must also be considered. 1 µF capacitors can complement larger and smaller capacitors by helping shape the impedance response over particular frequency ranges. However, whether they effectively fill the gap between other capacitance values depends on the actual impedance curves, not just the nominal capacitance. 0.1 µF capacitors are commonly used for high-frequency decoupling near chip power pins. Although their capacitance is smaller, they can often be placed in compact packages with short connection paths, helping reduce parasitic inductance and improve high-frequency decoupling performance. Each has its strengths, and combining them can make sense. However, 10 µF, 1 µF, and 0.1 µF are not a universal combination with three fixed frequency ranges. Their effective operating ranges may overlap, and the appropriate values depend on the chip’s requirements, component characteristics, and PCB layout. （capacitor unit conversion chart） How Dielectric and Package Size Affect Decoupling （MLCC Package Size and Decoupling Performance） Two factors that deserve more attention than capacitance alone are dielectric material and package size. Let's start with the dielectric. Suppose you choose a 10 µF ceramic capacitor with a Y5V or Z5U dielectric because it is inexpensive and offers the desired nominal capacitance. Once operating conditions come into play, its capacitance may change significantly with temperature and DC bias voltage. That does not mean these dielectric types are unsuitable for every application. However, their characteristics may make them less suitable for decoupling applications that require stable capacitance. For common power supply decoupling applications, X7R and X5R are often preferred dielectric types. But choosing either one does not guarantee that the nominal capacitance will be available under operating conditions. Multilayer ceramic capacitors (MLCCs), especially those with high capacitance in small packages, can experience significant capacitance loss under DC bias. Always check the manufacturer's datasheet, particularly the DC bias curve, to determine how much effective capacitance remains at the actual operating voltage. For example, a nominal 10 µF X5R capacitor may provide substantially less capacitance at a particular operating voltage and package size. Even if several capacitors are installed, the effective decoupling capacitance may still be insufficient. Now, let's look at package size. Two 0.1 µF capacitors in 0402 and 0805 packages may have different parasitic characteristics and high-frequency performance. Under otherwise comparable conditions, a smaller package can help reduce component parasitics and the inductance of the mounting loop. However, the actual improvement depends on the component structure, terminal design, and PCB layout. You cannot assume that ESL decreases by a fixed percentage every time the package size is reduced. Sometimes, optimizing the package size and mounting loop can be more effective than simply increasing capacitance. That said, smaller is not always better. Capacitance requirements, voltage rating, soldering reliability, and manufacturing constraints must also be considered. How Parasitics and Anti-Resonance Affect PCB Decoupling Some designers assume that if capacitors with different values can cover different frequency ranges, adding more of them should suppress noise across the board. That sounds reasonable in theory, but reality is more complicated. When multiple capacitors are connected in parallel, their capacitance, ESR, ESL, and PCB interconnect parasitics interact to form a complex impedance network. Under certain conditions, this network can produce an anti-resonance peak, causing the impedance of the power distribution network to rise at a particular frequency. In simple terms, some capacitor branches may behave capacitively while others behave inductively at that frequency. Their interaction, together with interconnect parasitics, can create an impedance peak. The peak's frequency and magnitude depend on the component parameters, connection topology, PCB power planes, and mounting loops. Simply adding or removing capacitors does not guarantee a solution. PCB space is also limited. Adding too many capacitors can crowd routing areas and force some components farther away from the chip's power pins. Longer connection paths can increase loop inductance and weaken high-frequency decoupling performance. So, do not focus only on how many capacitors appear in the schematic. Where they are placed, how they are connected, and how the overall network behaves are equally important. Consider a design example. Suppose a simulation of an FPGA power distribution network reveals a pronounced anti-resonance peak. Adding more capacitors with different capacitance values may not solve the problem and could even make the peak more pronounced. A better approach is to examine the impedance curve, analyze the capacitors' ESR and ESL, evaluate interconnect parasitics, and review the layout. The capacitor combination and connection topology can then be adjusted as needed. In some cases, a more optimized design may use fewer capacitors. However, removing capacitors without checking the impedance response can also increase impedance in certain frequency ranges. The real goal is not to minimize the number of capacitors, but to optimize the impedance of the entire power distribution network. PCB Decoupling Capacitor Design: Three Key Principles It comes down to three key principles. 1. Start with the requirements, not guesswork. For high-speed digital circuits, the target impedance method can help guide decoupling design: Here, (Delta V) is the allowable power supply voltage variation, and (Delta I) is the transient current change that the power distribution network must support. First, determine the allowable voltage variation based on the chip's power requirements. Then estimate the target impedance and evaluate the required capacitance values, capacitor count, and placement based on the load's transient behavior and the PDN impedance profile. Of course, target impedance is only one part of the design process. Voltage regulator response, chip packaging, PCB power planes, and the actual capacitor characteristics must also be considered. Rather than copying a fixed capacitor combination, start by understanding what the circuit actually needs. 2. Placement matters more than quantity. A decoupling capacitor should be placed as close as practical to its corresponding chip power pin. The current loop between the power pin, capacitor, and ground plane should be kept short. Connect the capacitor's ground terminal to a continuous ground plane through a via placed as close to the ground pad as practical. For high-frequency decoupling, multiple ground vias may help reduce loop inductance, depending on the layout and current path. However, two vias are not mandatory in every design. Also, proximity alone does not guarantee a good layout. Poor power routing, an indirect ground path, or an unsuitable via connection can still introduce significant parasitic inductance. Remember: High-frequency decoupling is not just about placing a capacitor close to the chip. It is about creating a short, low-inductance current loop. This is one of the most important considerations in decoupling capacitor placement and effective PCB layout. 3. Know when to simplify—but do not remove capacitors blindly. Not every chip needs the full 0.1 µF, 1 µF, and 10 µF combination. For low-speed circuits with modest transient current demands, a small number of decoupling capacitors may be sufficient, provided the device requirements are met. High-speed FPGAs, processors, and other devices with demanding transient loads may require a more complex capacitor network and a carefully designed power distribution system. The appropriate number and values of capacitors should be determined using the chip manufacturer's recommendations, target impedance, and design verification results. A well-designed network is more reliable than a collection of capacitors added without a clear purpose. （Good vs. Poor Decoupling Capacitor Placement） The 0.1 µF, 1 µF, and 10 µF combination is a useful engineering starting point, not a universal rule. There is a sound reason behind it: capacitors with different capacitance values have different impedance characteristics, and a suitable combination can improve power distribution network performance across different frequency ranges. But that does not mean more capacitance is always better—or that fewer capacitors automatically make a better design. Good power supply design is not about how many capacitors you solder onto a board. It is about understanding frequency, impedance, component characteristics, and PCB layout . Do not simply copy a reference design and place capacitors without understanding why they are there. Learn to evaluate the actual requirements and make informed design decisions. Sometimes, the problem is not that you need more capacitors. It is that the wrong capacitor was selected—or the first one was placed incorrectly. Less guesswork, more deliberate design. That is the principle behind effective decoupling capacitor selection and PCB power integrity. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Are More PCB Decoupling Capacitors Always Better? by: Mila Oct 12,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout decoupling capacitor PCB decoupling capacitor decoupling capacitor placement PCB power integrity If you have ever designed a PCB schematic , you have probably placed a familiar trio of capacitors near a chip’s power pins: 0.1 µF, 1 µF, and 10 µF.It seems like a safe bet. Different capacitance values, neatly arranged, ready to keep the power supply stable and suppress noise. But is this tried-and-tested combination always the best choice? When it comes to decoupling capacitors, does adding more always mean better performance? Not necessarily. Effective decoupling depends on more than capacitance alone. Component characteristics, parasitic effects, and PCB layout all play a role. Understanding ESR, ESL, and Self-Resonant Frequenc Circuit theory tells us that the impedance of an ideal capacitor decreases as frequency increases. Real capacitors, however, are not quite so simple. They have two important parasitic parameters: equivalent series resistance (ESR) and equivalent series inductance (ESL). ESL deserves particular attention. As frequency increases, the capacitive impedance decreases until the capacitor reaches its self-resonant frequency (SRF). Around this frequency, the capacitor typically exhibits its minimum impedance. Beyond SRF, parasitic inductance begins to dominate, and impedance increases with frequency. In other words, a capacitor does not become more effective at filtering noise simply because the frequency keeps rising. Above its SRF, its ability to suppress higher-frequency noise may be limited. That is why selecting a PCB decoupling capacitor requires more than checking its nominal capacitance. You also need to understand how its impedance changes with frequency. How Different Capacitance Values Work Together Capacitors with different capacitance values have different impedance characteristics. When selected appropriately, they can help maintain low impedance across a wider frequency range in the power distribution network (PDN). 10 µF capacitors are commonly used to provide local charge storage and help reduce impedance over certain low- to mid-frequency ranges. Their actual performance depends on the capacitor type, package, ESR, ESL, and operating voltage. For lower-frequency ripple, the voltage regulator, bulk capacitors, and the overall power network must also be considered. 1 µF capacitors can complement larger and smaller capacitors by helping shape the impedance response over particular frequency ranges. However, whether they effectively fill the gap between other capacitance values depends on the actual impedance curves, not just the nominal capacitance. 0.1 µF capacitors are commonly used for high-frequency decoupling near chip power pins. Although their capacitance is smaller, they can often be placed in compact packages with short connection paths, helping reduce parasitic inductance and improve high-frequency decoupling performance. Each has its strengths, and combining them can make sense. However, 10 µF, 1 µF, and 0.1 µF are not a universal combination with three fixed frequency ranges. Their effective operating ranges may overlap, and the appropriate values depend on the chip’s requirements, component characteristics, and PCB layout. （capacitor unit conversion chart） How Dielectric and Package Size Affect Decoupling （MLCC Package Size and Decoupling Performance） Two factors that deserve more attention than capacitance alone are dielectric material and package size. Let's start with the dielectric. Suppose you choose a 10 µF ceramic capacitor with a Y5V or Z5U dielectric because it is inexpensive and offers the desired nominal capacitance. Once operating conditions come into play, its capacitance may change significantly with temperature and DC bias voltage. That does not mean these dielectric types are unsuitable for every application. However, their characteristics may make them less suitable for decoupling applications that require stable capacitance. For common power supply decoupling applications, X7R and X5R are often preferred dielectric types. But choosing either one does not guarantee that the nominal capacitance will be available under operating conditions. Multilayer ceramic capacitors (MLCCs), especially those with high capacitance in small packages, can experience significant capacitance loss under DC bias. Always check the manufacturer's datasheet, particularly the DC bias curve, to determine how much effective capacitance remains at the actual operating voltage. For example, a nominal 10 µF X5R capacitor may provide substantially less capacitance at a particular operating voltage and package size. Even if several capacitors are installed, the effective decoupling capacitance may still be insufficient. Now, let's look at package size. Two 0.1 µF capacitors in 0402 and 0805 packages may have different parasitic characteristics and high-frequency performance. Under otherwise comparable conditions, a smaller package can help reduce component parasitics and the inductance of the mounting loop. However, the actual improvement depends on the component structure, terminal design, and PCB layout. You cannot assume that ESL decreases by a fixed percentage every time the package size is reduced. Sometimes, optimizing the package size and mounting loop can be more effective than simply increasing capacitance. That said, smaller is not always better. Capacitance requirements, voltage rating, soldering reliability, and manufacturing constraints must also be considered. How Parasitics and Anti-Resonance Affect PCB Decoupling Some designers assume that if capacitors with different values can cover different frequency ranges, adding more of them should suppress noise across the board. That sounds reasonable in theory, but reality is more complicated. When multiple capacitors are connected in parallel, their capacitance, ESR, ESL, and PCB interconnect parasitics interact to form a complex impedance network. Under certain conditions, this network can produce an anti-resonance peak, causing the impedance of the power distribution network to rise at a particular frequency. In simple terms, some capacitor branches may behave capacitively while others behave inductively at that frequency. Their interaction, together with interconnect parasitics, can create an impedance peak. The peak's frequency and magnitude depend on the component parameters, connection topology, PCB power planes, and mounting loops. Simply adding or removing capacitors does not guarantee a solution. PCB space is also limited. Adding too many capacitors can crowd routing areas and force some components farther away from the chip's power pins. Longer connection paths can increase loop inductance and weaken high-frequency decoupling performance. So, do not focus only on how many capacitors appear in the schematic. Where they are placed, how they are connected, and how the overall network behaves are equally important. Consider a design example. Suppose a simulation of an FPGA power distribution network reveals a pronounced anti-resonance peak. Adding more capacitors with different capacitance values may not solve the problem and could even make the peak more pronounced. A better approach is to examine the impedance curve, analyze the capacitors' ESR and ESL, evaluate interconnect parasitics, and review the layout. The capacitor combination and connection topology can then be adjusted as needed. In some cases, a more optimized design may use fewer capacitors. However, removing capacitors without checking the impedance response can also increase impedance in certain frequency ranges. The real goal is not to minimize the number of capacitors, but to optimize the impedance of the entire power distribution network. Of course, target impedance is only one part of the design process. Voltage regulator response, chip packaging, PCB power planes, and the actual capacitor characteristics must also be considered. Rather than copying a fixed capacitor combination, start by understanding what the circuit actually needs. 2. Placement matters more than quantity. A decoupling capacitor should be placed as close as practical to its corresponding chip power pin. The current loop between the power pin, capacitor, and ground plane should be kept short. Connect the capacitor's ground terminal to a continuous ground plane through a via placed as close to the ground pad as practical. For high-frequency decoupling, multiple ground vias may help reduce loop inductance, depending on the layout and current path. However, two vias are not mandatory in every design. Remember: High-frequency decoupling is not just about placing a capacitor close to the chip. It is about creating a short, low-inductance current loop. Not every chip needs the full 0.1 µF, 1 µF, and 10 µF combination. For low-speed circuits with modest transient current demands, a small number of decoupling capacitors may be sufficient, provided the device requirements are met. High-speed FPGAs, processors, and other devices with demanding transient loads may require a more complex capacitor network and a carefully designed power distribution system. The appropriate number and values of capacitors should be determined using the chip manufacturer's recommendations, target impedance, and design verification results. A well-designed network is more reliable than a collection of capacitors added without a clear purpose. （Good vs. Poor Decoupling Capacitor Placement） The 0.1 µF, 1 µF, and 10 µF combination is a useful engineering starting point, not a universal rule. There is a sound reason behind it: capacitors with different capacitance values have different impedance characteristics, and a suitable combination can improve power distribution network performance across different frequency ranges. But that does not mean more capacitance is always better—or that fewer capacitors automatically make a better design. Good power supply design is not about how many capacitors you solder onto a board. It is about understanding frequency, impedance, component characteristics, and PCB layout . Do not simply copy a reference design and place capacitors without understanding why they are there. Learn to evaluate the actual requirements and make informed design decisions. Sometimes, the problem is not that you need more capacitors. It is that the wrong capacitor was selected—or the first one was placed incorrectly. Less guesswork, more deliberate design. Verify Now Blog > Flex PCB Design Guidelines for Reliable Bending Flex PCB Design Guidelines for Reliable Bending by: Mila Oct 15,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout flex PCB design flex PCB bend radius flexible PCB design guidelines Unlike rigid PCBs, flexible PCBs (FPCs) can bend and fold to fit into compact electronic devices. They are widely used in smartphones, laptops, printers, and other products where space is limited or components need to move. However, flexibility does not mean an FPC can bend without limits. Poorly designed bend areas can lead to copper trace cracks, delamination, or premature failure, especially in applications involving repeated bending. A reliable flex PCB design must account for bend radius, trace routing, copper foil selection, and stiffener placement. In this guide, we’ll look at the key design considerations for FPC bend areas and how to improve their reliability in both static and dynamic bending applications. Three Common Flex PCB Bend Area Design Mistakes 1. Keep Vias Out of the Bend Area Vias are one of the key structures to watch when designing a flex PCB bend area. To simplify routing, inexperienced designers may place vias close to a bend line to change layers. However, repeated bending can eventually cause trace fractures and electrical failures. The reason is straightforward: vias introduce structural transitions between the copper plating, pads, and substrate. Differences in material properties and geometry can affect local stress distribution. During repeated bending, stress may concentrate around the via, leading to copper fatigue and crack propagation over time. Eventually, the electrical connection may fail. Design tip: Avoid placing through-holes, blind vias, or buried vias within the active bend area. If layer transitions are necessary, move the vias outside the bend area whenever possible. The required clearance depends on the bend geometry, board thickness, and manufacturer guidelines. A clearance of at least 1 mm can serve as an initial layout reference, but it is not a universal requirement for every FPC. 2. Components are relatively rigid, while the flexible substrate deforms during bending. If a component sits within the bend area, additional mechanical stress may develop around its body, pads, and solder joints. Brittle components, such as ceramic capacitors, require particular attention because both solder joint cracking and component body damage are possible. Design tip: Place components in rigid sections or reinforced areas, away from the actual bending region. A clearance of 2 mm beyond the bend boundary can serve as an initial reference, but the final distance should account for component size, stiffener geometry, and the actual bending range. 3. Do Not Choose Trace Direction Based on Routing Convenience Alone Trace direction affects how mechanical stress is distributed during bending. However, no single routing angle is best for every FPC structure. When routing through a bend area, consider the actual bending axis, bending direction, and trace distribution. Avoid sharp corners, abrupt width changes, and locally crowded traces, as these features can create stress concentrations. Traces perpendicular to the bending axis: This arrangement may be appropriate for traces crossing the bend area in certain single-axis bending structures, but it must be evaluated against the actual bending geometry. Traces parallel to the bending axis: Whether this arrangement is suitable depends on the specific structure. It should not automatically be classified as the most failure-prone direction. Traces at 45°: Angled routing may work in certain layouts, but its bending life cannot simply be assumed to fall between that of perpendicular and parallel traces. A relatively small bend radius may be acceptable, provided it meets the requirements of the specific material and structure. Dynamic bending: The FPC repeatedly bends during operation. Examples include foldable phone hinges, printer head cables, and robotic joints. These applications place greater demands on copper fatigue resistance, bend radius, and overall structural design. Keep vias and components out of active bend areas, route traces smoothly, allow sufficient bend radius, and select copper foil carefully for dynamic applications. For products that undergo repeated bending, validate the design through testing rather than relying on general rules of thumb alone. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > Flex PCB Design Guidelines for Reliable Bending Flex PCB Design Guidelines for Reliable Bending by: Mila Oct 15,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout flex PCB design flex PCB bend radius flexible PCB design guidelines Unlike rigid PCBs, flexible PCBs (FPCs) can bend and fold to fit into compact electronic devices. They are widely used in smartphones, laptops, printers, and other products where space is limited or components need to move. However, flexibility does not mean an FPC can bend without limits. Poorly designed bend areas can lead to copper trace cracks, delamination, or premature failure, especially in applications involving repeated bending. A reliable flex PCB design must account for bend radius, trace routing, copper foil selection, and stiffener placement. In this guide, we’ll look at the key design considerations for FPC bend areas and how to improve their reliability in both static and dynamic bending applications. Three Common Flex PCB Bend Area Design Mistakes 1. Keep Vias Out of the Bend Area Vias are one of the key structures to watch when designing a flex PCB bend area. To simplify routing, inexperienced designers may place vias close to a bend line to change layers. However, repeated bending can eventually cause trace fractures and electrical failures. The reason is straightforward: vias introduce structural transitions between the copper plating, pads, and substrate. Differences in material properties and geometry can affect local stress distribution. During repeated bending, stress may concentrate around the via, leading to copper fatigue and crack propagation over time. Eventually, the electrical connection may fail. Design tip: Avoid placing through-holes, blind vias, or buried vias within the active bend area. If layer transitions are necessary, move the vias outside the bend area whenever possible. The required clearance depends on the bend geometry, board thickness, and manufacturer guidelines. A clearance of at least 1 mm can serve as an initial layout reference, but it is not a universal requirement for every FPC. 2. Keep Components Out of the Bend Area Resistors, capacitors, ICs, connectors, and other SMT components should generally not be placed in areas that undergo repeated bending. Components are relatively rigid, while the flexible substrate deforms during bending. If a component sits within the bend area, additional mechanical stress may develop around its body, pads, and solder joints. Brittle components, such as ceramic capacitors, require particular attention because both solder joint cracking and component body damage are possible. Design tip: Place components in rigid sections or reinforced areas, away from the actual bending region. A clearance of 2 mm beyond the bend boundary can serve as an initial reference, but the final distance should account for component size, stiffener geometry, and the actual bending range. 3. Do Not Choose Trace Direction Based on Routing Convenience Alone Trace direction affects how mechanical stress is distributed during bending. However, no single routing angle is best for every FPC structure. When routing through a bend area, consider the actual bending axis, bending direction, and trace distribution. Avoid sharp corners, abrupt width changes, and locally crowded traces, as these features can create stress concentrations. Traces perpendicular to the bending axis: This arrangement may be appropriate for traces crossing the bend area in certain single-axis bending structures, but it must be evaluated against the actual bending geometry. Traces parallel to the bending axis: Whether this arrangement is suitable depends on the specific structure. It should not automatically be classified as the most failure-prone direction. Traces at 45°: Angled routing may work in certain layouts, but its bending life cannot simply be assumed to fall between that of perpendicular and parallel traces. For dynamic flex PCB applications, prioritize smooth, continuous traces, avoid sharp turns and abrupt geometry changes, and verify reliability through appropriate bending tests. (flex PCB bend area design with via and component keepout zones) How to Choose the Right Flex PCB Bend Radius When designing an FPC, some engineers focus mainly on whether it fits inside the enclosure. Reducing the bend radius too much may make assembly easier, but it can also shorten the product's service life. First, distinguish between static and dynamic bending. Their design requirements are different. Static bending: The FPC is bent during assembly and then remains in a relatively fixed position. Internal cables that do not move during normal operation are typical examples. A relatively small bend radius may be acceptable, provided it meets the requirements of the specific material and structure. Dynamic bending: The FPC repeatedly bends during operation. Examples include foldable phone hinges, printer head cables, and robotic joints. These applications place greater demands on copper fatigue resistance, bend radius, and overall structural design. For preliminary flex PCB design, the following values can serve as starting points: Static bending: A minimum bend radius of approximately 6 times the total board thickness may be used as an initial reference. Dynamic bending: A minimum bend radius of approximately 10 times the total board thickness or greater may be used as an initial reference. These ratios are not universal standards. The actual requirement depends on factors such as single-sided or double-sided construction, copper layer count, copper foil type, material thickness, and the target number of bending cycles. For applications requiring a long flex life, follow the design guidelines provided by the material supplier or FPC manufacturer. For example, if an FPC has a total thickness of 0.2 mm, the preliminary reference values would be: Static bend radius: 0.2 × 6 = 1.2 mm Dynamic bend radius: 0.2 × 10 = 2.0 mm These figures illustrate the calculation method only. They should not be treated as minimum design limits for every 0.2 mm FPC. An excessively small bend radius can cause copper fatigue cracking, coverlay or substrate delamination, and, in severe cases, substrate damage. Any of these failures can eventually render the flexible circuit unusable. RA Copper vs. ED Copper for Flex PCBs Copper foil is an essential part of the FPC's conductive structure and a key factor in repeated-bending reliability. When choosing copper foil, consider whether the application involves static or dynamic bending rather than focusing on cost alone. Electrodeposited copper (ED copper): ED copper is produced through an electrodeposition process and offers mature manufacturing processes and cost advantages. Its grain structure differs from that of rolled copper, and its fatigue performance should be evaluated carefully for repeated-bending applications. For applications involving relatively few bending cycles, ED copper may be considered depending on the specific design and manufacturer recommendations. Rolled-annealed copper (RA copper): RA copper is produced through rolling and annealing. It generally offers good ductility and flexing performance, making it suitable for FPCs that require a longer dynamic flex life. Although it typically costs more, it may help improve reliability in applications involving repeated bending. The key takeaway is simple: For static applications, select copper foil based on cost and performance requirements. For dynamic applications with high cycle counts, RA copper is generally the preferred starting point, subject to verification of the bend radius, copper thickness, and target service life. Flex PCB Routing Guidelines for Reliable Bending In addition to the major design restrictions discussed above, several details deserve attention during flex PCB routing and layout. Trace direction: Determine the routing direction based on the actual bending axis and motion. Traces should remain smooth and continuous, with unnecessary sharp turns avoided. Trace width and spacing: Choose appropriate trace widths and spacing to meet electrical and manufacturing requirements. Distribute multiple traces evenly across the bend area instead of crowding them into one section. The final dimensions should account for the bending structure, copper thickness, and manufacturing capabilities rather than relying on a fixed width-to-spacing ratio. Corners and width transitions: Use rounded corners or smooth transitions wherever practical. Avoid sharp corners and abrupt changes in trace width to reduce stress concentrations. Minimize unnecessary crossovers and layer transitions within the bend area. Coverlay: Flexible coverlay is commonly used to protect copper traces in bend areas and reduce the risk of wear and oxidation. Position coverlay openings carefully, keeping coverlay edges away from regions of high mechanical stress. Confirm the required coverage and manufacturing details for the specific design. FPC Stiffeners: Stainless Steel vs. PI Stiffeners increase local rigidity in an FPC. They are commonly used beneath connectors, gold fingers, and SMT components. However, stiffeners should not extend into the active bend area where the FPC needs to flex freely. Stainless steel stiffeners: Stainless steel provides relatively high rigidity and is commonly available in thicknesses of approximately 0.1–0.3 mm. It is often used behind connectors and gold fingers to improve structural support and withstand insertion and removal forces. Pay attention to edge geometry and transitions to prevent sharp edges from damaging the FPC substrate. PI stiffeners: Polyimide (PI) stiffeners are generally thinner and more flexible than metal stiffeners. They can be used beneath certain SMT components or in areas that require localized reinforcement while retaining some flexibility. Their actual rigidity depends on the material thickness and structure. Stress concentrations near stiffener edges should also be considered. Regardless of the stiffener type, keep it outside the active bend area. The required clearance depends on the bending range, stiffener thickness, and overall structure. A fixed 2 mm clearance alone cannot guarantee a reliable design. Static vs. Dynamic Flexing: Key Design Differences Design factorStatic bendingDynamic bendingBend radiusApproximately 6× board thickness as an initial reference; verify the designApproximately 10× board thickness or greater as an initial reference; verify the designCopper foilSelect according to cost and performanceRA copper is generally preferred for high-cycle applicationsLayer countSelect according to electrical and mechanical requirementsMinimize layer count where practical; single- or double-sided designs are often preferredTrace directionDetermine based on the bending geometryDetermine based on the actual motion and bending axisVias and componentsAvoid within the active bend areaAvoid within the active bend areaCoverlayDesign according to structural and protection requirementsPay particular attention to coverlay edges and repeated-bending reliabilityStiffenersPlace outside the active bend areaKeep outside the active bend area and manage edge-related stressTypical applicationsFPCs bent during assembly and then fixed in placeFoldable phones, printer head cables, robotic joints, and other moving assemblies Flex PCB Bend Area Design Checklist Before submitting your FPC design files, use the following checklist to review the bend area: No vias, including through-holes, blind vias, or buried vias, are placed within the bend area. No components or pads unsuitable for bending are placed within the bend area. Trace direction has been evaluated based on the actual bending axis and motion. Traces use smooth transitions without sharp corners or abrupt width changes. Multiple traces are distributed evenly to avoid local congestion. The copper foil type matches the static or dynamic bending requirements. The bend radius has been calculated and checked against material and manufacturer requirements. Layer count, copper thickness, and structural design have been evaluated for high-cycle applications. Coverlay openings and edges are positioned away from high-stress regions. Stiffeners remain outside the active bend area, with appropriate edge transitions. A suitable flex-life test plan has been established for critical dynamic applications. Ultimately, successful flex PCB design comes down to controlling bending strain, minimizing local stress concentrations, and ensuring that the materials and structure meet the required flex life. Keep vias and components out of active bend areas, route traces smoothly, allow sufficient bend radius, and select copper foil carefully for dynamic applications. For products that undergo repeated bending, validate the design through testing rather than relying on general rules of thumb alone. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac.
